title: Recover from errors

outcomes.can: Throw a specific exception for input a method cannot accept.
Catch one exception type and let others through.
Return a result value for an expected failure instead of throwing.

intro: Some failures are bugs, and some are expected: text that is not a number, a store that is offline. This module covers throwing and catching exceptions, and returning a result value when a failure is a normal outcome.

steps.title: Throw and catch
steps.text: An exception is an object that reports a failure. throw new ArgumentException("Minutes cannot be negative."); stops the current method at once and passes the exception to its caller. If nothing catches it, the program stops. A try block marks code that may fail, and a catch block after it runs only when an exception of the named type is thrown inside the try. catch (FormatException) catches that type and no other. Naming a variable, as in catch (ArgumentException error), lets you read error.Message. Some built-in methods throw: int.Parse("soon") throws a FormatException because the text is not a number.

steps.title: Catch a bad format
steps.text: ReadMinutes is called with text that is a number and text that is not. Predict the first two lines of output.

steps.title: Follow both calls
steps.text: int.Parse("30") works, so the try block returns 30 and the catch never runs. int.Parse("soon") throws a FormatException. The rest of the try block is skipped, the catch block runs and returns -1. The caller sees an ordinary return value in both cases.

steps.title: What runs after a throw?
steps.text: Check(-5) throws inside the second try block. Predict the last line of output.

steps.title: Follow the exception
steps.text: Check throws, so it ends at once. Back in the try block, the line that prints "checked" is skipped, because control jumps straight to the matching catch. That block prints the exception's Message. Catch the most specific type you can handle. catch (Exception) catches everything, including bugs you would want to see, so it is rarely the right choice.

steps.title: Expected failures can be values
steps.text: An exception suits a failure the caller is not expected to handle on every call, such as a broken promise about the input. When failure is a normal outcome, a return value is often clearer. A result type holds either the answer or the reason there is none, for example record Parsed(bool Ok, int Minutes, string Error). The caller reads Ok and cannot forget that failure is possible. Built-in methods offer the same choice. int.TryParse(text, out int value) returns false for bad text instead of throwing.

steps.title: Reject negative minutes
steps.text: The starter accepts every input. Make it throw for the input it cannot accept.

steps.title: Parse minutes into a result
steps.text: Work from the prompt. The method must never throw for the inputs listed.

review.evidence: Open a fresh starter on a later visit, with the earlier answer closed. A first unaided pass on every case is later evidence of the skill. A hinted pass stays recorded as assisted.

drillGap: These drills practise one statement each. They do not check which exception types are caught and which pass through.
